questions.solution:
· Sound waves are mechanical waves that require a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to propagate.

· In a vacuum, there is no medium for sound waves to travel through.

· Therefore, the statement that sound waves can travel through a vacuum is incorrect.

The wavelength of a sound wave is defined as the distance between two consecutive compressions or two consecutive rarefactions.

It is usually represented by λ (lambda) and measured in meters.

· In the diagram, A represents the wavelength, which is the distance between two consecutive crests or troughs of a wave.

· Wavelength is a measure of the spatial period of the wave.

A sound wave is the pattern of disturbance caused by the movement of energy traveling through a medium (such as air, water or any other liquid or solid matter) as it propagates away from the source of the sound.

A mechanical wave is transverse when all the particles of the medium, which are solid or liquid (and never gas), vibrate perpendicularly at right angles, up and down, and continue to move in the direction of the wave. For example, the ripples on the surface of a lake are transverse waves. Sound does not move through transverse waves except in special conditions.

Frequency (ν) is defined as the number of complete oscillations per unit time.

It is measured in hertz (Hz), where 1 Hz = 1 oscillation per second.

questions.question: The unit of frequency is: आवृत्ति की इकाई है:
questions.solution:
The SI unit of frequency is hertz (Hz), named after Heinrich Rudolph Hertz.

One hertz equals one cycle per second.

questions.solution:
Sound propagation follows this sequence:

o Vibration of the source.

o Vibration of particles in the medium.

o Disturbance travels through the medium.

o Sound reaches the ear.

The quality or timbre of sound is that characteristic which enables us to distinguish one sound from another having the same pitch and loudness.

It depends on the number of overtones present in the sound and their relative intensities.

· Sound waves are called mechanical waves.

· Sound waves require a medium for propagation.

Both statements are true, and the reason correctly explains why sound waves are mechanical waves.

Sound travels fastest in solids, followed by liquids, and then gases. This is because the particles in solids are closely packed and can transmit vibrations more efficiently.

At a particular temperature, sound travels fastest in iron compared to water and air.

The audible range of sound for human beings extends from about 20 Hz to 20000 Hz (20 kHz).

Sounds below 20 Hz are called infrasound, and those above 20 kHz are called ultrasound.

The sensation of sound persists in our brain for about 0.1 s. For a distinct echo, the time interval between original and reflected sound must be at least 0.1 s.

At 344 m/s, sound travels 34.4 m in 0.1 s.

Since sound must travel to the obstacle and back, the minimum distance to the reflecting surface is 34.4 m ÷ 2 = 17.2 m.
The time taken for one complete oscillation of the density or pressure of the medium is called the time period or period of the sound wave. It is represented by the symbol T and measured in seconds.

Sounds with frequencies higher than 20 kHz are called ultrasonic sound or ultrasound.

These sounds are beyond the audible range of humans but can be heard by certain animals like bats and dolphins.

Reverberation is the persistence of sound in a big hall due to repeated reflections from the walls, ceiling, and floor.

Unlike an echo, which is a distinct repetition of the original sound, reverberation causes sound to continue until it is reduced to an inaudible level.

The speed (v), frequency (ν), and wavelength (λ) of sound are related by the equation v = λ X ν.

This equation shows that speed equals wavelength multiplied by frequency.

Using the formula,

Speed = frequency x wavelength = 500 Hz x 0.7 m = 350 m/s

When sound travels from one medium to another, its frequency remains unchanged.

The speed and wavelength change according to the properties of the new medium, but the frequency is a characteristic of the source and remains constant.

The quality or timbre of sound is that characteristic which enables us to distinguish one sound from another having the same pitch and loudness. For example, the sound of a violin and a flute may have the same pitch and loudness but can be distinguished by their quality.

Ultrasonography is based on the principle of reflection of ultrasound waves. In this technique, ultrasonic waves travel through the tissues of the body and get reflected from regions where there is a change in tissue density.

These reflected waves are then converted into electrical signals to generate images.

To reduce reverberation in auditoriums, the walls and ceiling are generally covered with sound-absorbent materials like compressed fiberboard, rough plaster, or draperies.

These materials absorb sound energy rather than reflecting it, preventing excessive reverberation.
